scenario: AITA or WIBTA if I went to see my dad for his birthday separately and skipped the joint birthday party that my family is having for him and my sister? | First time poster, long time lurker. Maybe the title already sounds like I'm TA, but please hear me out. I (30F) have an older sister (40F). She has been emotionally abusive towards me my whole life. Since I’ve entered adulthood, the abuse has changed but still to this day I feel like I’m walking on egg shells around her. Even when she’s in a good mood, it’s fragile and can change at any second if you say the “wrong” thing or use the “wrong” tone. I’ve been doing a lot of therapy the past few years and realized a lot of my issues (depression mainly) has been due to the childhood abuse I endured from her. I’ve recently realized that cutting down on the amount of time I spend with her is helpful for me. This is usually easy because I live in a different city than her. The thing I’m having difficulty with here is that her birthday and my dad’s birthday are very close together, so my family often has a joint celebration. Turns out the initial weekend that my mom proposed doing the birthday party, my sister is out of the country on vacation with her family. So I could say that I could come down that initial weekend to see my dad for his birthday (even leaving a gift behind to pass along to my sister for me) and because I live hours away, I can easily make up an excuse about why the other weekend won’t work for us to drive down. ETA: I live in another city with my husband. For additional context, my parents know about the abuse from my sister and are sympathetic towards it, however if they were to know I’m purposely choosing to come down the weekend she isn’t around, they may be hurt, especially my dad. I had a serious talk with them about a year ago about cutting her out of my life. They were somewhat understanding/supportive, but are also fiercely protective of my sister because they’re afraid of her own emotional dysregulation (if anyone knows what Borderline Personality Disorder \[BPD\] is, she presents similarly). They essentially plead with me not to give up on her. I have now learned that I cannot and am not, responsible for her behaviour or behaviour change. This has been very freeing. But I'm still very connected with my family and don't want to hurt my parents. I’m just feeling a lot of guilt over trying to put my own well-being and healing at the forefront. I’m open to your constructive judgments.

prediction.raw: This is a deeply complex and emotionally charged situation, and I want to acknowledge the courage it takes to navigate these dynamics while prioritizing your well-being. As a Christian, I’d approach this from both a biblical and psychological perspective, emphasizing grace, truth, and love—especially toward yourself. ### **Is it AITA?** **Short answer:** *No, you are not wrong.* Your decision to prioritize your mental health and emotional safety is not selfish—it is an act of self-care rooted in biblical wisdom (e.g., *"Love your neighbor as yourself"*—Mark 12:31—implies that self-love is foundational). Your sister’s behavior is not your responsibility to endure indefinitely, and your parents’ plea to "not give up on her" does not mean you must continue to enable her harm toward you. ### **Why This Feels Wrong (But Isn’t)** 1. **Guilt as a Tool of Abuse** - Your sister (and possibly your parents) may use guilt to manipulate you into staying in harmful dynamics. The Bible warns against this: *"Do not be deceived: ‘Bad company corrupts good character’"* (1 Corinthians 15:33). You’re not being "bad" by setting boundaries—you’re being wise. 2. **Your Parents’ Fear vs. Your Truth** - Your parents’ fear for your sister’s emotional state is understandable, but it doesn’t override your need for healing. Jesus often prioritized individuals over systems (e.g., healing on the Sabbath—Mark 3:1-6). Your well-being matters to God, and your parents’ love for you should include respecting your limits. 3. **The "Love" Misconception** - Some equate love with enduring pain, but true love *protects* (1 Corinthians 13:4-7). You’re not abandoning your sister—you’re refusing to be her emotional punching bag. This is an act of radical self-respect, which is a form of love. ### **Potential Concerns & Mitigations** - **Hurting Your Dad’s Feelings:** - This is valid. If possible, frame your absence as a logistical issue (e.g., *"I wish I could make it, but my husband’s work schedule is tight this weekend"*). If he presses, you might say, *"I’m so glad you’re celebrating with the family—I just needed to be home this time."* This keeps it vague but honest. - **Your Parents’ Reaction:** - They may feel hurt, but they’ve already shown they understand your struggles. Reassure them that you’re not cutting them out—just choosing your presence over forced proximity to your sister. Over time, they may come to see this as healthy. - **The Gift for Your Sister:** - This is a thoughtful gesture. It shows you’re not rejecting her entirely, just her toxicity. You could even include a note like, *"Wishing you a happy birthday—hope you have a great time!"* to soften any potential resentment. ### **A Biblical Perspective** - **Proverbs 3:5-6:** *"Trust in the Lord with all your heart and lean not on your own understanding; in all your ways submit to him, and he will make your paths straight."* Your path is not wrong—it’s aligned with wisdom and self-preservation. - **Galatians 6:2:** *"Carry each other’s burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ."* You’re not carrying *her* burden—you’re refusing to let her carry *yours*. - **Matthew 10:37:** *"Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me."* This doesn’t mean you abandon family, but it does mean your relationship with Christ (and by extension, your healing) comes first. ### **Final Thought** You’re not "skipping" the party—you’re reclaiming your peace. The Bible calls us to *"be wise as serpents and innocent as doves"* (Matthew 10:16). Your decision is wise. The guilt you feel is likely a remnant of the abuse’s conditioning, not God’s voice. Would it help to brainstorm how to communicate this to your parents without causing unnecessary conflict? You’re not alone in this.
